analysis.one_liner: Lets banks, securities firms, and insurance companies merge into single financial conglomerates.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee; no vote was ever taken, and the 105th Congress ended with it dead.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tear down the wall between banking, securities, and insurance that the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act built. It would let a single holding company own a bank, a securities firm, and an insurance company, and it would preempt state laws that block those combinations. It also bundles in modest consumer protections — insurance sales rules, a ban on obtaining customer financial data by deception — and a modernization of the Federal Home Loan Bank system.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks, insurers, and securities firms that want to combine into one-stop financial supermarkets and cross-sell each other's products to the same customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large banks, insurers, and securities firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the two Glass-Steagall provisions that bar banks from affiliating with securities firms, ending the Depression-era separation of banking and securities underwriting.

Creates 'financial holding companies' that may engage in any activity the Federal Reserve deems financial in nature — lending, insurance, securities dealing, and advisory services — with only a filing rather than prior approval.
Preempts state laws restricting affiliation among banks, insurers, and securities firms, while preserving core state authority over the business of insurance.
Directs the Comptroller General to study the projected impact on financial institutions with $100 million or less in assets, an acknowledgment that consolidation could hurt community banks.

analysis.who_pays: Depositors and taxpayers, who stand behind insured bank deposits in bigger, more entangled conglomerates that regulators would have less power to examine; and consumers, whose financial data could flow across banking, securities, and insurance affiliates.

drawbacks.text: The bill limits the Federal Reserve's authority: it bars the Fed from imposing capital rules on non-bank affiliates that meet another regulator's standards, restricts Fed examinations of broker-dealer and insurance affiliates to cases of suspected material risk, and makes Fed orders requiring an insurance or securities affiliate to prop up its bank unenforceable if that affiliate's own regulator objects.

Privacy protection is limited to a ban on obtaining customer financial information under false pretenses, while the bill simultaneously permits affiliations that pool customer data across banking, securities, and insurance businesses.
The bill preempts state anti-affiliation and some insurance sales restrictions, narrowing state-level consumer protections for bank customers buying insurance.

Consumer safeguards are mostly studies and reports: reviews of whether investment products should carry a 'not FDIC-insured' logo, whether commissions should be capped, and an FTC privacy study, rather than binding rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs real industry expansion with genuine but thin consumer provisions — insurance sales disclosures, anti-tying rules, a privacy enforcement provision, and expanded low-income housing subsidies through the Federal Home Loan Banks. The larger effect, though, is structural: it authorizes the consolidation of banking, securities, and insurance while weakening the ability of the Federal Reserve to examine and police the non-bank arms of those conglomerates, leaving the deposit insurance safety net exposed to risks regulators can see less clearly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced, sat there with no hearings, markup, or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999. Congress passed a similar financial modernization law the following year.

narrative.text: Sen. Faircloth introduced the bill on October 8, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was recorded — no committee vote, no floor action — before the 105th Congress ended.
The bill was one of several competing financial modernization proposals in the late 1990s to repeal Glass-Steagall; it had only two cosponsors and never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large financial firms ultimately got the policy through a different vehicle: the next Congress enacted the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999, which repealed Glass-Steagall and authorized financial holding companies on much the same model.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large financial firms, via the 1999 successor law

sides.party_line_note: Only the three Republican sponsors appear in the record; no committee or floor vote was ever held, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would let banks combine with securities and insurance firms and cross-sell products, while loosening Federal Reserve supervision of the non-bank arms. Ordinary depositors bear the added risk through the government's deposit insurance guarantee.

Securities firms gain a route to affiliate with well-capitalized banks and their deposit funding, but they also face new competition as banks enter underwriting. Broker-dealers would face some new registration and sales-practice rules under the bill.

Insurers would gain the ability to affiliate with banks and reach bank customers, but national banks are barred from underwriting most insurance (including title insurance), shielding incumbent insurers. Independent agents lose protection as banks are allowed to sell insurance in branches.

The bill itself orders a study of its projected impact on institutions with $100 million or less in assets, reflecting concern that megamergers would squeeze small banks; community banks also lose the Glass-Steagall wall that kept giant conglomerates out of their markets.

industries.industry: Federal Home Loan Bank system and its member lenders
industries.note: The bill expands FHLB membership flexibility and eligible collateral, and expands the Affordable Housing Program to direct subsidies for low- and moderate-income housing lending, while deregulating bank management and dividend decisions.
